title: The world’s largest instrument, says Guinness, is an organ that taps cave stalactites

cover.alt: The Great Stalacpipe Organ’s console standing in a lit chamber of Luray Caverns, surrounded by hanging stalactites and flowstone.

body: Deep in Luray Caverns, Virginia, the Great Stalacpipe Organ makes music by striking **37 stalactites** with solenoid-driven rubber mallets, each wired to a key on an organ-style console. Leland W. Sprinkle had the idea on a cave tour in 1954 and spent three years from 1956 building it, shaving selected stalactites down until each rang at the right pitch. The stalactites are spread over about 3.5 acres of the cavern, which is why Guinness World Records considers it the world’s largest instrument, and the sound can be heard anywhere in the cave’s 64 acres, even without loudspeakers. Technically it is a lithophone: an instrument played by striking stone.

slides.alt: A small solenoid with a rubber-tipped mallet mounted on a bracket beside a stalactite in Luray Caverns, with wiring running to it.
slides.caption: A solenoid-driven mallet poised beside its stalactite. Each one is wired to a single key of the console.

slides.question: How many stalactites does the organ play?
slides.explanation: 37, each shaved to tune it to a particular note. Sprinkle built the mechanism over three years from 1956; Klann Organ Supply of Waynesboro made the console.

slides.heading: The organ spreads across the cave
slides.note: The organ can be heard anywhere in the 64-acre cavern, even without loudspeakers.

steps.label: A key is pressed on the console
Current fires a solenoid by the stalactite
A rubber mallet taps the stone
The stalactite rings through the cave

slides.question: What kind of instrument is the Stalacpipe Organ, technically?
slides.explanation: A lithophone is played by striking stone. Despite the name there are no pipes: the ‘pipes’ are stalactites hit by mallets.

slides.heading: Tuning a cave
slides.text: Sprinkle chose stalactites whose natural pitch was close to what he needed, then shaved them to tune them precisely. The console originally had pedal-operated volume switching and draw-knobs labelled Pedal, Harmonic, Solo and Echo; these were later removed in favour of a constant level of amplification.
